li.a: The Jewish Independent: Geoffrey Edelsten, the Jewish doctor who made medicine glitzy and grubby
The Guardian: Geoffrey Edelsten, high profile former doctor and one-time Sydney Swans owner, dies at 78
The Sydney Morning Herald: The fall and rise to riches of Edelsten and his young bride
Nine News: Geoffrey Edelsten dead, controversial businessman dies aged 78
The Sydney Morning Herald: Geoffrey Edelsten files for US bankruptcy

content.p: Geoffrey Edelsten spent decades in the Australian public eye as a doctor who treated medicine as showbusiness. He built a chain of lavish 24-hour clinics, bought a football club, married women decades younger than himself and drove cars with number plates such as "macho", "spunky" and "sexy". In 1990 a Supreme Court jury found him guilty of soliciting a notorious hit man, Christopher Dale Flannery, to assault a former patient, and he was also convicted of perverting the course of justice. He served a year in prison. He died alone in a Melbourne apartment on 11 June 2021, aged 78.
content.h2: A Carlton boy with a record label
content.p: Edelsten was born in Carlton, Melbourne, on 2 May 1943 to Jewish migrant parents. The Jewish Independent describes an unremarkable Melbourne Jewish upbringing: Princes Hill Primary, then Mount Scopus College, then medicine at the University of Melbourne, where he graduated in 1966. His grandparents on both sides had come from Eastern Europe. In a 2010 profile the Sydney Morning Herald reported that his parents built a lingerie retail chain, Linda Leigh, and eventually settled in Toorak.

Even as a student he was looking for deals. He ran a record company, Hit Productions, and is listed as co-writer of two songs for a band called The Last Straws. He later co-produced a single, "Love Machine", for a studio group featuring Glenn Shorrock, who went on to front the Little River Band. After graduating he worked as a resident at the Royal Melbourne Hospital and then as a country doctor, with Nine News naming Birchip in western Victoria and Wauchope in New South Wales, where he learned to fly. In 1971, according to the Jewish Independent, he and a partner founded Preventicare, a company offering diagnostic tests and computerised history-taking to doctors. The newspaper says the idea was sound but the finances were not, and it lasted only a few months. His friend and former business partner Tom Wenkart later described him to the Herald as colourful, extreme and "not liked by the profession in general", and as a "very slow payer" who was "pretty flippant about cash flow".

When the federal government introduced Medicare in 1984, Edelsten's clinics embraced bulk-billing. The Jewish Independent calls them the first in Australia to do so. They stayed open around the clock and had chandeliers, grand pianos in the foyers and mink-covered examination tables. At his peak, that paper reports, he owned 13 centres whose 200 doctors saw 20,000 patients a week. The Herald's 2010 profile said he turned general practice "from a cottage industry into a slick commercial enterprise".

The money paid for a life to match. He married his first wife, Leanne Nesbitt, a 20-year-old model-turned-nurse, in 1984, when he was 41. Nine News reported that for her 21st birthday he reportedly gave her a pink sports car. The next year he took over the Sydney Swans.

In 1985 the VFL wanted its first privately owned club, and Edelsten emerged as the successful bidder for the financially strapped Sydney Swans. The reported price was $6.3 million, and Nine News said the purchase cleared the club's debts. He signed big names, among them Greg Williams, who would win the 1986 Brownlow Medal, and the coach Tom Hafey. The Jewish Independent says the Swans became the talk of Sydney and filled the SCG.

How much of his own money went into the deal is unclear. The same article says many at the club believed he was a front man for a company called Westeq, which put up the cash. He was removed as chairman before the end of the 1986 season, around the time the New South Wales Rugby League rejected his bid to buy the Cronulla Sharks. Edelsten himself, according to the Guardian, described his part as that of a "white knight" for a club facing dire financial pressure. He remained a Carlton supporter, and the club made him a life member in 2013.

After the Swans, the empire unravelled. The Herald's 2010 profile says that by 1988 he had been bankrupted, deregistered and divorced. In New South Wales he was removed from the medical register in 1988. Nine News and the Jewish Independent both give the reason as the use of unqualified staff to carry out laser surgery. The Herald adds that he was found guilty of professional misconduct that included inducing doctors on his staff to over-service patients. He was deregistered in Victoria four years later, according to the Herald.

The criminal case came from his link to Flannery, a man known as a hit man. Edelsten told the Herald he had come to know Flannery while removing a tattoo. He gave his own account of the relationship in that interview: that Flannery once told him he charged $50,000 to kill people and $10,000 to bash them, which Edelsten treated as a funny story. According to the Herald, a man who had been treated at one of Edelsten's clinics began a campaign of threats and harassment against him, and Edelsten phoned Flannery. He has always insisted, the paper wrote, that he merely wanted advice and that Flannery told him to call the police.

A jury did not accept that. In 1990 a Supreme Court jury found him guilty of soliciting Flannery to assault the former patient. The Herald reports that he was also convicted of perverting the course of justice: he had issued Flannery a medical certificate that allowed a murder trial to be postponed, so that a particular judge was avoided. The Guardian dates the soliciting verdict to 1990, and the Jewish Independent says he was sent to prison for a year that year.

Edelsten described the sentence to the Herald as "life-changing and shattering". He was sent to Long Bay, which he called a season in hell, saying he was next to murderers and men serving 20-year sentences, with Neddy Smith "two cells" away. He was later moved to a low-security prison where, he said, inmates spent the day making crutches. A brain scan soon after his release revealed a large tumour, which the paper says proved benign and was removed.

The Herald also spoke to Max Donnelly, the bankruptcy trustee who had to sell Edelsten's clinics and divide the proceeds among creditors, chief among them the tax office. Donnelly, who said he had dealt with crime boss Robert Trimbole and the fugitive Christopher Skase, called Edelsten "totally unco-operative" and harder to deal with than either. By Donnelly's account the network of 32 clinics had been built on borrowed money: Edelsten would make the first payment on each loan and then stop. "Everyone thought he was a man of great substance but there wasn't really a lot behind it," Donnelly said.

The Herald wrote that Edelsten believes the financial problems, the convictions and the loss of his licence were all undeserved; of his deregistration he said doctors who worked for him had given "the most atrocious lies as evidence, to protect their backsides". The paper also reported that in 1998 he was forced into a scheme of arrangement with his creditors after borrowing more than he could repay, and that he kept calling himself Dr Edelsten after deregistration. It noted that the professorship and PhD on his website came from Pacific Western University, an unaccredited Californian school identified in a US government report as a diploma mill. Edelsten told the Herald he had worked hard for the PhD and held an adjunct professorship before the university was discredited.
content.h2: Comeback, weddings and a second fall
content.p: In 2005 he and business partners founded Allied Medical Group. The Jewish Independent says it was sold in 2011 to the American company Sonic Healthcare in a deal reportedly worth $200 million. In 2010 Edelsten told the Herald that Allied employed close to 250 GPs at 17 clinics, and the paper reported that he had a major interest in the group.

His private life drew as much coverage as his business. In 2009, at 67, he married Brynne Gordon, a 26-year-old American fitness instructor, at Melbourne's Crown Casino; the ceremony was reported to have cost more than $3 million. The Jewish Independent notes that the 550-guest event featured a chuppah and a ceremony conducted by the actor Jason Alexander. The marriage ended in late 2013, and in June 2015 he married the 24-year-old American model Gabi Grecko, per Nine News. They separated for good in 2019, after years of on-and-off headlines.

The money, meanwhile, was running out. In January 2014, the Sydney Morning Herald reported, he declared himself bankrupt in an Ohio court, one day before a hearing in a long-running fight with his former United States partners, the Mawardi family, over a clothing brand, a casino in the Dominican Republic, an aircraft and a pair of slum housing complexes. His petition listed debts of $18.2 million and said he was worth between US$10 million and US$50 million. Creditors included the Australian Taxation Office, US tax authorities, National Australia Bank, his own mother and Marina Bay Sands. His Australian lawyers called it a strategy to "better realise the investments made in the US". The Guardian reports that he also claimed bankruptcy in Australia that year and that by 2016 more than 40 creditors were chasing him. In 2019, it adds, he escaped penalty after police stopped him driving an unregistered car in Melbourne.

Edelsten died on Friday 11 June 2021 at an apartment on St Kilda Road. The Guardian reported that Victoria Police prepared a report for the coroner and did not treat the death as suspicious. The Jewish Independent wrote that he had lived as a virtual recluse for his last few months. Greg Williams, the Brownlow medallist he had brought to the Swans, told a radio station that people had an opinion of Edelsten but that he was "a lot different than the actual opinion". Brynne Edelsten's spokesman said she was deeply saddened.
